subject: physics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Einstein's photoelectric equation is best written as:
questions.explain: hf = φ + ½mv²max: photon energy equals the work function plus the maximum kinetic energy of the electron.

questions.q: A sample has a half-life of 8 days. What fraction remains after 24 days?
questions.explain: 24 days is three half-lives, so (1/2)^3 = 1/8 of the sample remains.

questions.q: The greater the binding energy per nucleon, the:
questions.explain: Higher binding energy per nucleon indicates a more tightly bound, more stable nucleus.

questions.q: The relationship between half-life T-half and decay constant lambda is:
questions.explain: Setting N = N0/2 in the decay law gives T-half = ln2/lambda.

questions.q: Which harmonics are present in a pipe closed at one end?
questions.explain: A closed pipe supports only odd harmonics (1st, 3rd, 5th...) because of the node-antinode boundary conditions.

questions.q: Alpha radiation is typically stopped by:
options: a few cm of air or paper
questions.explain: Alpha particles are absorbed by a sheet of paper or a few centimetres of air.

questions.q: Why does photoelectric emission occur almost instantaneously when light above the threshold frequency strikes a metal?
options: A single photon delivers all its energy to one electron at once
questions.explain: A photon transfers its energy to a single electron in one interaction, so emission is essentially instantaneous.

questions.q: Which radiation is the most penetrating?
questions.explain: Gamma rays are highly penetrating, requiring thick lead or concrete to attenuate.

questions.q: The fact that R is proportional to A^(1/3) implies that nuclear density is:
questions.explain: Mass is proportional to A and volume to R^3 (i.e. A), so density is roughly constant across nuclei.

questions.q: In a double-slit experiment, slit separation is 0.50 mm, the screen is 2.0 m away and the fringe spacing is 2.4 mm. What is the wavelength of the light?
The de Broglie hypothesis applies to:
options: All moving particles, though the effect is significant only for very small masses
questions.explain: All moving matter has a de Broglie wavelength λ = h/p, but it is only measurable for tiny masses like electrons.

questions.q: Two waves are described as coherent. This means they have:
options: A constant phase difference and the same frequency
questions.explain: Coherent sources maintain a constant phase difference and have the same frequency.

questions.q: The principle of superposition states that when two waves meet, the resultant displacement is:
options: The product of the individual displacements
The vector sum of the individual displacements
The larger of the two displacements
questions.explain: Superposition states the resultant displacement equals the (vector) sum of the individual displacements.

questions.q: Mass defect is defined as the:
options: difference between the mass of the constituent nucleons and the nucleus
questions.explain: Mass defect is the difference between the total mass of separate nucleons and the assembled nucleus.

questions.q: In the photoelectric effect, increasing the intensity of light above the threshold frequency increases:
options: The maximum kinetic energy of emitted electrons
The number of electrons emitted per second
questions.explain: Higher intensity means more photons per second, so more electrons are emitted, but their maximum KE is unchanged.

questions.q: The activity of a radioactive sample is given by:
questions.explain: Activity equals the decay constant multiplied by the number of undecayed nuclei, A = lambda N.

questions.q: One electronvolt (1 eV) is equal to:
questions.explain: 1 eV is the energy gained by an electron accelerated through 1 V, equal to 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ J.

questions.q: On the N-Z stability graph, light stable nuclei lie:
options: close to the N = Z line
questions.explain: Light stable nuclei lie near N = Z; heavier ones need more neutrons (curve above the line).

questions.q: In a Young's double-slit experiment the fringe spacing w is given by w = λD/s. To increase the fringe spacing you could:
questions.explain: Since w = λD/s, longer wavelength (smaller frequency) increases the fringe spacing.

questions.q: A graph of maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons against frequency has a gradient equal to:
questions.explain: From KEmax = hf − φ, the gradient of KEmax against f is the Planck constant h.

questions.q: A nucleus above the stability line (neutron-rich) typically decays by:
questions.explain: Neutron-rich nuclei undergo beta-minus decay, converting a neutron to a proton.

questions.q: How many photons of wavelength 600 nm are needed to deliver 1.0 J of energy? (E ≈ 3.3 × 10⁻¹⁹ J per photon)
questions.explain: Number = total energy / photon energy = 1.0 / 3.3×10⁻¹⁹ ≈ 3.0×10¹⁸ photons.

questions.q: Monochromatic light of wavelength 600 nm strikes a grating with d = 2.0 × 10⁻⁶ m. At what angle does the first-order maximum appear?
Unpolarised light passes through two polarising filters whose transmission axes are at 90° to each other. The emergent intensity is:
questions.explain: Crossed polarisers (axes at 90°) block all the light, giving zero transmitted intensity.

questions.q: The y-intercept of a maximum-KE-versus-frequency graph for the photoelectric effect equals:
questions.explain: From KEmax = hf − φ, the intercept on the KE axis is −φ (negative of the work function).

questions.q: A microwave of frequency 12 GHz travels in air. Its wavelength is approximately (c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s):
The ionisation energy of an atom is the energy needed to:
options: Completely remove an electron from the atom in its ground state
Excite an electron to the next level
questions.explain: Ionisation energy is the energy required to remove an electron entirely (to the n = ∞, zero-energy level) from a ground-state atom.

questions.q: When light reflects off the surface of water, the reflected light becomes partially polarised. This demonstrates that light is:
questions.explain: Only transverse waves can be polarised, so polarisation on reflection confirms light is transverse.
